feedback: If your partner rebuilds the picture correctly from the digits, you have shown that a picture is just an agreed pattern of 0s and 1s.
If the rebuilt picture is wrong, compare your grid to the digits row by row to find where a 0/1 was misread — a good way to see how precise the shared system must be.
When asked about more colours: a single 0/1 only distinguishes two states, so extra colours force extra digits per pixel.
activities.intendedInsight: A picture can be reduced to a grid of two-state pixels, so images, numbers and text can all be represented as patterns of two symbols. With one binary digit a pixel can only be two colours; more colours need more digits per pixel. Which digit stands for black is an agreed convention, not a fixed fact — the same point the whole topic makes.
learnerActions: Decode a grid of 0s and 1s (by an agreed convention here 0 = white, 1 = black) by colouring the matching squares, and watch a picture emerge.
Draw your OWN small black/white picture on a grid (e.g. a 5×6 letter 'C'), then write the binary digits for each pixel.
Hand your binary to a partner and have them rebuild the picture from your digits alone.
Discuss: if you wanted more than two colours per pixel, what would you need to add?
activities.title: Pictures are patterns too: the black/white pixel grid
